stages.walkthrough: I'll assume generated output can be automatically executed and tested in Replit's own environment, and that task complexity varies from simple single-page apps to multi-component applications. Plan: brief why-AI/system-design context, then focus mainly on the eval framework, since 'does the generated app actually work' is the central question, closing with metrics.

Building even a simple application from scratch requires translating a natural-language intent into working code across multiple interacting steps, which is exactly the kind of open-ended, context-dependent task a fixed template generator can't handle beyond the most common, pre-anticipated app shapes — this is a case where the value clearly requires generative capability, not a deterministic alternative, since the space of possible requested applications is effectively unbounded.

A hobbyist prototyping a simple idea has high tolerance for the agent needing a few iterations to get right, since the stakes of an early wrong attempt are low and iteration is cheap. A user building something with real users or data (even a small app) has lower tolerance for subtle correctness bugs that pass a superficial 'it runs' check but produce wrong behavior under some inputs. A non-technical user who can't read the generated code to verify it has the lowest tolerance of all, since they have no independent way to catch an error the agent itself doesn't surface.

The agent should be evaluated (and ideally operate) as a loop, not a single generation: generate, execute in the sandboxed environment, observe errors or test failures, and iterate — since a single-shot generation for a multi-step task has a much higher failure rate than an iterative one that can self-correct against real execution feedback. This iterative design is itself a system-design choice with direct eval implications: success should be measured at the end of the iteration loop, not on the first draft.

The agent should show its iteration steps visibly (what it's building, what errors it hit, what it changed) rather than presenting only a final result, since that transparency is what lets a technical user catch a wrong turn early instead of only discovering a subtle bug after the fact. For the non-technical-user segment, a plain-language summary of what was built and a simple way to describe what's wrong in their own words (rather than pointing at code) is the main correction path. On a task the agent can't complete after reasonable iteration, the fallback is to say so honestly and show what it has so far, rather than presenting an incomplete or broken result as finished.

A golden set of task descriptions paired with automated test suites checking actual functional behavior (not just 'does it run without a crash'), since a plausible-looking app that doesn't do what was asked is a more insidious failure than one that visibly crashes. LLM-as-judge is weak here for the same reason as any code-generation eval: correctness is objectively checkable by running tests, so the eval should prioritize automated test-pass rate over a judge model's subjective read of whether the code 'looks right.' For the non-technical-user segment specifically, I'd add a distinct eval checking whether the agent explains what it built in plain language, since that user has no other way to sanity-check the result.

North Star candidate: task-completion rate on held-out tasks, defined strictly as passing the task's automated test suite, not merely 'produced runnable code,' which would reward plausible-but-wrong output. Guardrails: rate of tasks that run without crashing but fail their functional tests (the specific insidious-failure category called out above), average iterations-to-success (a proxy for efficiency, not just eventual correctness), and cost per successfully completed task, since an iterative agent loop can run many expensive generation-and-execution cycles per task.

pitfalls: Treating 'the generated app runs without crashing' as sufficient evidence of correctness, missing the more insidious case of code that runs but doesn't do what was asked
Judging output quality by how plausible the code looks rather than by actually executing it against real functional tests
